WP-SHELLSTORM webshell drop (down.php / obfuscated PHP) under wp-content AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence outcome of the mass-exploitation: a PHP webshell (notably down.php, a 4-layer-obfuscated BestShell derivative) written into wp-content/plugins, /themes, or /uploads by the web-server process itself — the tell of an exploit-driven upload rather than an admin install. Article-specific via the down.php filename and the WordPress content-directory write path. Rationale: Uses the named webshell down.php and the WordPress content-dir write path, gated on the web-server account writing PHP (exploit upload signature) rather than a legitimate admin install; corroborated by SOCRadar and eSecurityPlanet describing down.php dropped under wp-content. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/wp-shellstorm-exposed-hackers-backdoored-thousands-of-wordpress-websites/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate plugin/theme install or auto-update via wp-admin (files written by php-fpm to /plugins/ with a valid manifest)
  • WP-CLI plugin installs run by an administrator on the host
  • Caching plugins (Breeze, BerqWP) writing PHP cache artifacts into wp-content
  • Developer deploying custom plugin code via SFTP as the web-server user
  • Backup/restore tooling repopulating wp-content
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("wp-cli","wp plugin install","wp theme install") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the dropped .php and check for the WP-SHELLSTORM markers (nested @eval, base64_decode, gzinflate, str_rot13) and whether it was written by php-fpm/nginx with no matching plugin update in wp-admin logs. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the webshell, take the site offline or into maintenance, reset all WordPress admin + DB credentials, and patch the entry-point plugin (Breeze to 2.4.5, JCE to 2.9.99.5, and the other listed CVEs). 3) Hunt: grep the whole webroot for sibling shells, review access logs for POSTs to the dropped filename and the source IPs, and check for the php-spawns-shell and [kworker/0:2] follow-on activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "wp-content"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/plugins/","/themes/","/uploads/") or FileName =~ "down.php"
| where FileName endswith ".php"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe") or FileName =~ "down.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has "wp-content"
| where (TargetFilePath has_any ("/plugins/","/themes/","/uploads/") and TargetFileExtension =~ "php") or TargetFileName =~ "down.php"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp") or TargetFileName =~ "down.php"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WordPress Webshell File Drop under wp-content (WP-SHELLSTORM down.php)
id: 7c2a91d4-6e0b-4f83-9a11-2d5c8b7e4a02
description: Detects a PHP file written into a WordPress content directory by the web-server process, or a file named down.php - the WP-SHELLSTORM webshell persistence outcome.

  - https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1505.003
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/wp-content/plugins/'
      - '/wp-content/themes/'
      - '/wp-content/uploads/'
    TargetFilename|endswith: '.php'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/down.php'
  condition: selection_path or selection_name
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/wp-content\/(plugins|themes|uploads)\/.*\.php$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(php-fpm|php|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp)/i OR TargetFileName=/\/down\.php$/i

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*wp-content*" AND Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="*.php" AND (Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/plugins/*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/themes/*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/uploads/*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="down.php") by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*wp-content*" AND Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="*.php" AND (Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/plugins/*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/themes/*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path="*/uploads/*" OR Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name="down.php") by Endpoint.Filesystem.dest Endpoint.Filesystem.file_name Endpoint.Filesystem.file_path Endpoint.Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Filesystem)` | sort - lastTime
Web-server process spawning a shell/downloader (PHP webshell RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the execution phase of a live webshell: php-fpm/httpd/nginx spawning sh, bash, curl, wget or nc — the behaviour of down.php's shell_exec/proc_open running attacker commands or fetching the SNOWLIGHT dropper. Article-specific because the webshell's stated capabilities are 'run commands, open reverse shells, scan the network'. Rationale: Anchors on the exact parent (web-server) to child (shell/downloader) tree that a PHP webshell produces when running commands or pulling SNOWLIGHT; the webshell's command-execution and reverse-shell capability is stated directly in the article. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/wp-shellstorm-exposed-hackers-backdoored-thousands-of-wordpress-websites/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • WP-Cron or plugin code legitimately shelling out to sendmail/imagemagick/curl for feeds
  • Site backup plugins invoking mysqldump via shell_exec
  • Server-management panels (cPanel, Plesk) running maintenance under the web user
  • CI/CD deploy hooks executing as the nginx/php user
  • Image-processing plugins calling convert/ffmpeg
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/usr/sbin/sendmail","mysqldump","imagemagick","/usr/bin/convert"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child process command line — attacker recon looks like whoami/id/uname, network scans, or curl/wget to an external host; benign hits are bounded tool paths (sendmail, convert). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and hunt for the webshell file that the php parent loaded (correlate by DeviceId/time with the wp-content .php drop detection). 3) Hunt: pivot on any external IP/domain fetched by the child (feeds the C2 detection), and check for VShell installation ([kworker/0:2]) and new cron/systemd persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl","python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl","python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Server Process Spawning Shell or Downloader (PHP Webshell Execution)
id: 9e4c1b77-2a80-4d5f-b6c3-8a1f0e2d9c34
description: Detects php-fpm/httpd/nginx spawning a shell or network downloader, indicating live webshell command execution (WP-SHELLSTORM down.php).
references:
  - https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/php-fpm'
      - '/httpd'
      - '/apache2'
      - '/nginx'
      - '/php'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
  condition: selection
level: high
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(php-fpm|php|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|curl|wget|nc|ncat|perl|python3?)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")) AND (Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl","python","python3")) by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php-fpm","php","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe")) AND (Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl","python","python3")) by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - lastTime
VShell backdoor masquerading as [kworker/0:2] kernel thread AIInstallation High
Detects the WP-SHELLSTORM crew's own remote-access implant: VShell renames its process to [kworker/0:2] to blend with Linux kernel worker threads. Real kworkers are kernel threads that never carry an on-disk image, so any EDR process-create event whose name/cmdline is [kworker/...] but which has a real executable path is high-fidelity masquerading. Article-specific via the exact disguise string. Rationale: The [kworker/0:2] disguise is a named, exact IOC in the article; the detection exploits the invariant that genuine kernel worker threads never produce a process-create event with an on-disk image, so a filesystem-backed [kworker] is unambiguous masquerade. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://www.esecurityplanet.com/threats/wp-shellstorm-exposed-hackers-backdoored-thousands-of-wordpress-websites/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1055
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin/pentester deliberately spoofing a process name during a red-team exercise
  • Container runtimes surfacing host kernel-thread names in unusual telemetry mappings
  • Poorly-written monitoring agent that prctl-renames itself to a kworker-like string
  • Custom kernel modules exposing helper userland processes with kworker naming (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the FolderPath/SHA256 of the process backing the fake [kworker/0:2] and its parent — legit kernel threads have empty image and parent kthreadd; a real path plus outbound sockets confirms VShell. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill and preserve the binary for analysis, and reset any credentials that could have been harvested from the box. 3) Hunt: pivot on the binary's outbound connections (WebSocket C2 / the SNOWLIGHT chain), check other WordPress/Java hosts for the same masqueraded process, and map to UNC5174 SNOWLIGHT->VShell tradecraft.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "[kworker/" or FileName startswith "[kworker"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "["   // real kernel threads have no on-disk image; a filesystem path = userland masquerade
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "[kworker/" or ActingProcessName startswith "[kworker"
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: VShell Process Masquerading as Linux kworker Kernel Thread
id: 1a6f8b3c-4d92-4e07-9c5a-7b2e1f0d6a45
description: Detects a userland process disguised as [kworker/...] with a real executable path - the VShell implant masquerade used by WP-SHELLSTORM operators.
references:
  - https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/exposed-hacker-server-reveals-wp.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

  - attack.t1055
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains: '[kworker/'
  filter_real_kthread:
    Image: ''
  condition: selection and not filter_real_kthread
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:*[kworker/* -@process.executable.path:""
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/\[kworker\//i
| ImageFileName=/.+/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process="*[kworker/*" AND Endpoint.Processes.process_path!="unknown" AND Endpoint.Processes.process_path!="" by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_path Endpoint.Processes.process Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.process="*[kworker/*" AND Endpoint.Processes.process_path!="unknown" AND Endpoint.Processes.process_path!="" by Endpoint.Processes.dest Endpoint.Processes.process_name Endpoint.Processes.process_path Endpoint.Processes.process Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - lastTime
C2 / tooling callback to WP-SHELLSTORM infrastructure (137.175.93.126, xxooonline.eu.cc) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host contacting the exposed WP-SHELLSTORM operator infrastructure — the C2/tooling server 137.175.93.126, secondary IP 43.108.17.80, or domain xs.xxooonline.eu.cc — indicating a compromised web server pulling tools or beaconing. Article-specific: these are the exact indicators tied to the exposed open-directory server. Rationale: 137.175.93.126 is the SOCRadar/Ctrl-Alt-Intel confirmed operator open-directory/C2 server; 43.108.17.80 and xs.xxooonline.eu.cc are the pre-extracted campaign indicators. Direct IOC match is inherently high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/wp-shellstorm-expose-1-4m-wordpress-sites/ • https://www.techrepublic.com/article/news-wp-shellstorm-wordpress-webshell-attack/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or the SOC's own threat-intel team deliberately connecting to the exposed server for analysis
  • Sandbox/detonation infrastructure resolving the domain during malware analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment pipelines pinging the IOC to validate liveness
  • A shared-hosting neighbour on the same VPS IP after reallocation (rare, verify port/service)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox","curl") and DeviceName has_any ("soc-","research-","sandbox-"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the source host — if it's php-fpm/nginx or the fake [kworker], treat as confirmed compromise; if it's a browser/research tool, benign. 2) Contain: block 137.175.93.126, 43.108.17.80 and *.xxooonline.eu.cc at the egress firewall/DNS sinkhole, isolate any endpoint that initiated the connection, and preserve netflow/pcap. 3) Hunt: sweep all web servers for the down.php webshell and [kworker] masquerade, review inbound access logs for the exploited plugin endpoints, and rotate credentials on any host that beaconed out.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("137.175.93.126","43.108.17.80") or RemoteUrl has "xxooonline.eu.cc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationIP in ("137.175.93.126","43.108.17.80") or DestinationHostName has "xxooonline.eu.cc" or RequestURL has "xxooonline.eu.cc"
 | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, DestinationPort, DeviceProduct),
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has "xxooonline.eu.cc"
 | project TimeGenerated, ClientIP, Name, IPAddresses=Result)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Network Connection to WP-SHELLSTORM C2 Infrastructure
id: 5d7e2c19-8b40-4a6f-91c3-2e9d1a7f0b56
description: Detects outbound connections to the exposed WP-SHELLSTORM operator server 137.175.93.126, secondary 43.108.17.80, or domain xs.xxooonline.eu.cc.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp:
      - '137.175.93.126'
      - '43.108.17.80'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd (@network.destination.ip:137.175.93.126 OR @network.destination.ip:43.108.17.80)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=/^(137\.175\.93\.126|43\.108\.17\.80)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
# log group: /aws/vpc/flowlogs
fields @timestamp, srcAddr, dstAddr, dstPort, action, bytes
| filter dstAddr in ["137.175.93.126","43.108.17.80"]
| sort @timestamp desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("137.175.93.126","43.108.17.80") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("137.175.93.126","43.108.17.80") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.process | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | sort - lastTime
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents

| where RemoteIP in ("137.175.93.126", "43.108.17.80") or RemoteUrl has_any ("xs.xxooonline.eu.cc")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["137.175.93.126", "43.108.17.80"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["xs.xxooonline.eu.cc"]);

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Study of 281 Free Android VPN Apps Finds Traffic Leaks, Unencrypted Data, and Tracking

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers ran 281 of the most popular free VPN apps on the Google Play Store through a new testing system and found that many fail at the basics people install a VPN for, i.e., keeping their traffic private and secure. The apps flagged with at least one problem have been installed more than 2.4 billion times. The problems are basic, not sophisticated. 29 apps let user traffic leak outside

CVEsCVE-2016-6329 CVE-2016-2183
ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Cleartext HTTP fetch of OpenVPN config file (tunnel-hijack exposure)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Free VPN app beaconing to advertising / analytics trackers
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DNS leak: mobile/VPN device querying public resolvers outside the tunnel · [LLM] VPN app sending user traffic in cleartext HTTP outside the tunnel · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Cleartext HTTP fetch of OpenVPN config file (tunnel-hijack exposure) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts managed/mobile devices that download an OpenVPN configuration file (.ovpn / config endpoint) over plaintext HTTP port 80 instead of HTTPS. The MVPNalyzer study showed five free VPN apps fetch their config in the clear, letting a same-network attacker rewrite it and repoint the tunnel at an attacker server. Rationale: Anchored on the article's most severe finding — five apps fetch their .ovpn config over cleartext HTTP, enabling tunnel rewrite. Matches GET of .ovpn/config endpoints on port 80.
ATT&CKT1557 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate enterprise VPN using an internal HTTP config-distribution portal on a trusted LAN
  • Captive-portal redirect returning a .ovpn download page over HTTP
  • MDM/EMM agent pulling a VPN profile from an internal HTTP repo
  • QA/test devices pointed at a staging VPN server over HTTP
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIP !startswith "10." and RemoteIP !startswith "192.168." and not (RemoteIP matches regex @"^172\.(1[6-9]|2[0-9]|3[0-1])\.")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the VPN app (InitiatingProcessFileName / package) and the config host; confirm the fetch was HTTP not HTTPS and whether the host is internal or internet-facing. 2) Contain: block the cleartext config host at the proxy/firewall and advise affected users to stop using the app until config delivery moves to HTTPS with cert validation. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for subsequent tunnel traffic to unexpected server IPs (config rewrite → attacker endpoint) and DNS/HTTP going to new destinations after the config fetch.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemotePort == 80
| where RemoteUrl has_any (".ovpn", "config.ovpn", "vpnconfig", "/config", "profile.ovpn")
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DestinationPort == 80
| where ApplicationProtocol has "http" or isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has_any (".ovpn", "config.ovpn", "vpnconfig", "/config", "profile.ovpn")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), SampleUrl=any(RequestURL) by SourceIP, DestinationIP, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

DNS leak: mobile/VPN device querying public resolvers outside the tunnel AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts devices sending DNS queries directly to well-known public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, OpenDNS, Quad9) while a free VPN app is installed — the study found 24 apps leak DNS, exposing visited sites to the local network. Surfaces resolver IPs a properly-tunneled client should never contact directly. Rationale: Anchored on the study's DNS-leak finding (24 apps, ~360M installs). Direct queries to the canonical public resolvers named in the reviewer hypothesis (8.8.8.8/1.1.1.1/OpenDNS) are the observable shape of a VPN failing to tunnel DNS.
ATT&CKT1590.002 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Devices legitimately configured to use 1.1.1.1/8.8.8.8 as primary DNS with no VPN in play
  • Corporate DoH/DoT fallback to public resolvers on network failure
  • Home/BYOD routers forwarding to public resolvers
  • Split-tunnel VPN policy that intentionally excludes DNS
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("dns.exe","systemd-resolved") and isnotempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the device has an active VPN app and whether DNS to the public resolver occurred while the tunnel was 'connected'; identify the app package. 2) Contain: enforce network-level DNS to corporate resolvers and block direct outbound port 53 to public IPs for managed devices. 3) Hunt: review the leaked query names for sensitive destinations and check whether the same device also leaked full browsing traffic (HTTP/HTTPS to non-VPN egress IPs).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 53
| where RemoteIP in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","208.67.222.222","208.67.220.220","9.9.9.9")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Queries=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by Queries desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ServerIPAddress in ("8.8.8.8","8.8.4.4","1.1.1.1","1.0.0.1","208.67.222.222","208.67.220.220","9.9.9.9")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count(), SampleNames=make_set(Name, 10) by Computer, ClientIP, ServerIPAddress
| order by Queries desc

Free VPN app beaconing to advertising / analytics trackers AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts VPN application processes on managed devices connecting to known ad/analytics networks — the study found 246 of 281 apps (>80%) contacted advertising/tracking servers and 76 exfiltrated the device Advertising ID. Surfaces a privacy-marketed VPN process talking to trackers it shouldn't need. Rationale: Anchored on the study's tracking finding (246 apps contact ad/analytics servers; 76 send the Advertising ID). Scopes tracker-domain contact to VPN/proxy-named processes so the signal is 'a privacy tool phoning trackers', not generic ad traffic.
ATT&CKT1567 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A bundled VPN feature inside a legitimate app suite whose process name contains 'vpn' and legitimately uses analytics with consent
  • In-app ad SDK activity users consented to
  • Enterprise VPN client sending crash/telemetry to a first-party analytics endpoint
  • Domain-fronting where a benign CDN resolves to a tracker apex
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the VPN app/package and which tracker domains it hit; determine if the app is on the study's flagged list and whether it was corporate-sanctioned. 2) Contain: block the tracker domains for managed devices and flag the app for removal via MDM if unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: check the same device for Advertising-ID/IMEI/email strings in outbound payloads and for GPS-coordinate exfil (the study noted one app sent exact coordinates).
let trackers = dynamic(["doubleclick.net","google-analytics.com","googlesyndication.com","graph.facebook.com","appsflyer.com","adjust.com","app-measurement.com","mixpanel.com","adcolony.com","applovin.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "vpn" or InitiatingProcessFileName has "proxy"
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (trackers)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Trackers=make_set(RemoteUrl, 15) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Hits desc

DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

VPN app sending user traffic in cleartext HTTP outside the tunnel AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts VPN/proxy-named processes originating plaintext HTTP (port 80) connections to public destinations — the study found 61 apps send data in plain text and 6 leaked full browsing traffic outside the encrypted tunnel. Surfaces a supposed 'encrypted tunnel' emitting readable, un-tunneled HTTP. Rationale: Anchored on the study's cleartext finding (61 apps send plaintext, 6 leak full browsing). A VPN process emitting un-tunneled public HTTP is the direct observable of the described leak/cleartext failure.
ATT&CKT1048.003 T1020
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VPN client performing an HTTP connectivity/captive-portal probe (e.g. to a status endpoint) by design
  • VPN app checking for updates over HTTP to a first-party host
  • Internal proxy appliance whose process name contains 'proxy' handling legitimate HTTP
  • Split-tunnel policy intentionally routing some HTTP directly
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "connectivitycheck" and RemoteUrl !has "captive" and RemoteUrl !has "/generate_204"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the process is a VPN/proxy app and inspect the cleartext HTTP destinations — distinguish a benign connectivity probe from actual user-data traffic. 2) Contain: if user data is leaving in cleartext, flag the app for removal via MDM and block its egress; advise users the tunnel is not protecting them. 3) Hunt: correlate with the same device's DNS-leak and tracker-beacon hits, and check whether the app also fetched its config over HTTP (tunnel-hijack exposure).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 80
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "vpn" or InitiatingProcessFileName has "proxy"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), Dests=dcount(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName
| where Connections > 0
| order by Connections desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 80
| where isnotempty(ProcessName) and (ProcessName has "vpn" or ProcessName has "proxy")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Connections=count(), Dests=dcount(DestinationIP) by SourceIP, ProcessName
| order by Connections desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2016-6329", "CVE-2016-2183")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Critical

Hackers Use Fake Microsoft Entra Passkey Enrollment to Gain Microsoft 365 Access

The Hacker News
2026-07-10 15 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A threat actor has been targeting organizations spanning multiple sectors with voice-based fake security requests that prompt Microsoft 365 users to enroll a new Entra passkey with an aim to carry out data extortion attacks. The threat actor, tracked by Okta under the moniker O-UNC-066, has deployed a panel-controlled phishing kit that's capable of targeting the passkey enrollment process. The

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Access to O-UNC-066 passkey-themed phishing kit domains · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Failed Entra sign-in burst followed by passkey-based success · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Entra ID passkey / FIDO2 security-key registration (O-UNC-066 rogue enrollment) · [LLM] Entra passkey enrollment from off-hours or never-before-seen IP · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Passkey registration immediately followed by passkey sign-in (rogue-enrollment account takeover) · [LLM] M365 sign-in with recently-enrolled passkey from new user-agent and IP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Entra ID passkey / FIDO2 security-key registration (O-UNC-066 rogue enrollment) AIInstallation Medium
Surfaces every passkey/FIDO2 authentication-method registration in Entra ID so an analyst can validate it against a legitimate rollout. O-UNC-066 vishes users into approving the attacker's own passkey against their Microsoft 365 account, so a registration event is the pivotal artifact of this campaign. Rationale: Anchored on the article's core TTP — the attacker enrolls their own passkey after phone-guided MFA approval; a passkey/FIDO2 method-registration audit event is the durable artifact. Broad by design (hunting tier) because Microsoft's own passkey registration campaigns generate the same event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/authentication/how-to-authentication-passkeys-fido2
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft/admin-driven passkey registration campaign nudging users to enroll (the article notes this feature coincides with the abuse)
  • Help-desk assisted passkey enrollment for a new hire
  • User self-enrolling a FIDO2 key from a corporate device during onboarding
  • Bulk FIDO2 provisioning via Graph/PowerShell (e.g. Token2 bulk enroll)
  • Passkey re-registration after device replacement
Suppression filter
| where ActorIP !in ("<corporate_egress_placeholder_do_not_use>") // prefer: exclude your admin bulk-enroll service principal by AccountObjectId once known
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the registering IP/UA and the target user; confirm the user actually initiated a passkey enrollment (call them out-of-band, do not use the same channel the attacker used). 2) Contain: if unrecognized, remove the newly-registered authentication method in Entra, revoke the user's refresh tokens/sessions, and force re-registration under a verified admin. 3) Hunt: check whether the same IP/UA registered passkeys for other users, and whether a passkey sign-in followed within minutes (see correlated UC).
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application in~ ("Microsoft Entra ID","Office 365","Azure Active Directory")
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","Passkey","security key")
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, UserAgent, RawEventData
| sort by Timestamp desc
let RegOps = dynamic(["User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User started security info registration","User completed security info registration","Add passkey"]);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where OperationName in~ (RegOps) or OperationName has "security info"
| where tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","Passkey","security key")
| extend Actor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, Result, ResultReason, Actor, ActorIP, TargetResources
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

source:azure.activeDirectory (@evt.name:"User registered security info" OR @evt.name:"Add passkey" OR @action:*security\ info*) (*Fido2* OR *FIDO2* OR *passkey* OR *Passkey* OR *security\ key*)
Access to O-UNC-066 passkey-themed phishing kit domains AIDelivery High
Detects DNS/network connections to the named O-UNC-066 phishing infrastructure whose domains all embed the word 'passkey' (and per-target subdomains). This is the delivery stage where the victim is steered to the operator-controlled PHP kit that mimics the Entra passkey enrollment flow. Rationale: Uses the five named IOC domains confirmed by Okta and BleepingComputer; `has_any`/endswith on the registrable domain also catches the per-target subdomains (e.g. exampleentity.setpasskey.com). Named, corroborated infrastructure = high fidelity, low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/ • https://www.technadu.com/o-unc-066-vishing-campaign-abuses-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment/630640/
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst intentionally browsing the IOC domain for analysis from a corporate host
  • Threat-intel sandbox/detonation VM resolving the domain
  • URL-scanning proxy or SWG pre-fetching the link
  • A benign passkey-vendor domain coincidentally matching the substring (verify exact registrable domain, not just substring)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and DeviceName !in~ ("soc-sandbox01","threat-detonation01")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user/host that resolved the domain and pull the surrounding sign-in and passkey-registration events for that user in the following hour. 2) Contain: block all five domains (and *.<domain>) at the SWG/DNS layer, revoke the user's tokens, and check for a newly-registered passkey to remove. 3) Hunt: sweep proxy/DNS org-wide for any of the five domains and for other passkey-substring domains registered recently; alert the user population targeted by the vishing calls.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| sort by Timestamp desc
let PkDomains = dynamic(["assignpasskey.com","deploypasskey.com","passkeydeploy.com","passkeyadd.com","setpasskey.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (PkDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Passkey registration immediately followed by passkey sign-in (rogue-enrollment account takeover) AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates an Entra passkey/FIDO2 method registration with a successful passkey-based sign-in by the same principal within 15 minutes. O-UNC-066 registers its own passkey and then immediately authenticates with it to take over the M365 account, so tight temporal linkage is high-fidelity. Rationale: Encodes the article's exact sequence: register attacker passkey, then use it. The 15-minute join eliminates the vast majority of benign enrollments (which are rarely used to sign in seconds later) and pins the takeover. RegIP vs sign-in IP surfaces the operator/victim split described in the kit walkthrough. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/hackers-use-fake-microsoft-entra.html
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User enrolls a passkey and legitimately tests it by signing in right away
  • Onboarding flow that enrolls then immediately authenticates the new key
  • Admin registers a key on behalf of a user during an assisted session and validates it
  • Conditional-access registration campaign that requires an immediate re-auth
Suppression filter
| where IPAddress != RegIP // keep only enroll-then-signin where the sign-in comes from a different IP than the registration
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare RegIP and sign-in IPAddress/geo — a mismatch or datacenter/VPN ASN strongly indicates the operator model described by Okta. 2) Contain: revoke sessions/refresh tokens, disable the account, and delete the just-registered passkey; require verified in-person/out-of-band re-enrollment. 3) Hunt: check the target app (Exchange/SharePoint/Teams) for post-auth mailbox rule creation, data access, or download bursts consistent with the data-extortion objective.
let Reg = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| project RegTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, RegIP = IPAddress;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey","Windows Hello")
| join kind=inner Reg on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (RegTime .. RegTime + 15m)
| project RegTime, SignInTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, RegIP, IPAddress, Country, Application, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, RegTime)
| sort by SignInTime desc
let Reg = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName has "security info" and tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| project RegTime = TimeGenerated, UserId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id), Upn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationMethodsUsed) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey","Windows Hello")
| join kind=inner Reg on $left.UserId == $right.UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (RegTime .. RegTime + 15m)
| project RegTime, SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, RegIP, IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', TimeGenerated, RegTime)
| sort by SignInTime desc
Entra passkey enrollment from off-hours or never-before-seen IP AIInstallation Medium
Flags passkey/FIDO2 registration events where the enrolling IP has not been seen for that user in the 30-day sign-in baseline, or the enrollment happens outside business hours. Targets the anomaly in the enrollment event itself rather than a follow-on sign-in. Rationale: Reviewer-requested anomaly view. The article's vishing calls occur opportunistically and the operator's IP will not match the victim's normal sign-in geography; a new-IP or off-hours passkey enrollment is a concrete deviation from legitimate self-service enrollment. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Traveling/remote employee enrolling a passkey from a hotel/home IP not in baseline
  • Shift worker or on-call staff enrolling legitimately at night
  • New hire whose IP baseline is thin/empty
  • Enrollment via corporate VPN egress that differs from prior sign-in IPs
  • Org-wide passkey campaign rolled out after hours to reduce user disruption
Suppression filter
| where NewIP == true // prioritize new-IP enrollments; drop the pure off-hours clause first if the org runs after-hours campaigns
Response runbook
1) Triage: geolocate RegIP and check the ASN — residential/VPN/datacenter far from the user's norm plus a recent vishing report escalates severity. 2) Contain: if unverified, delete the passkey, revoke tokens, and confirm with the user via a trusted channel. 3) Hunt: query AuditLogs for other passkey enrollments from the same RegIP/ASN across the tenant to find additional victims in the same campaign.
let Known = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize by AccountObjectId, IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","Register security information","Add passkey","security info")
| where tostring(RawEventData) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| extend HourUTC = hourofday(Timestamp)
| join kind=leftouter Known on AccountObjectId, IPAddress
| extend NewIP = isempty(IPAddress1)
| where NewIP or HourUTC >= 22 or HourUTC < 6
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, NewIP, HourUTC, ActionType
| sort by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 30d;
let KnownIPs = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(Lookback) .. ago(1d))
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserId, IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where OperationName has "security info" and tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| extend UserId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id), Upn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| extend HourUTC = hourofday(TimeGenerated), Day = dayofweek(TimeGenerated)
| join kind=leftouter (KnownIPs) on $left.UserId == $right.UserId, $left.RegIP == $right.IPAddress
| extend NewIP = isempty(IPAddress)
| where NewIP or HourUTC >= 22 or HourUTC < 6 or Day == 0d or Day == 6d  // off-hours (UTC) or weekend; adjust to org timezone
| project TimeGenerated, Upn, RegIP, NewIP, HourUTC, Day, OperationName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
Failed Entra sign-in burst followed by passkey-based success AIExploitation Medium
Detects an account with 3+ failed sign-ins in a 2-hour window that then produces a successful passkey/FIDO2 sign-in within 24 hours. Models the O-UNC-066 pattern of harvesting/validating credentials via the kit before the attacker-registered passkey grants durable access. Rationale: Ties the article's credential-harvesting kit (username/password captured to /backend.php) to the durable passkey outcome. A failed-auth cluster preceding a passkey success is a strong takeover shape that a plain passkey sign-in alone would miss. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.scworld.com/news/okta-warns-of-vishing-scheme-that-extorts-data
ATT&CKT1110 T1556.006
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User fat-fingers password several times then signs in with their legitimate passkey
  • Stale cached credentials on a second device causing failures before passkey use
  • Password-expiry period generating failures ahead of passwordless enrollment
  • MFA prompt timeouts logged as failures before a successful passkey auth
Suppression filter
| where SuccessIP !in (FailIPs) // keep cases where the passkey success comes from a different IP than the failed attempts
Response runbook
1) Triage: compare FailIPs to SuccessIP — different geo/ASN between the failures and the passkey success is the key escalator. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, disable the account, and audit the account's registered passkeys, removing any not verified with the user. 3) Hunt: pivot on FailIPs across the tenant for password-spray/enumeration against other users, and check for passkey registrations from those IPs.
let Failed = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode != 0
| summarize FailCount = count(), FailIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstFail = min(Timestamp) by AccountObjectId, AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 2h)
| where FailCount >= 3;  // 3+ failed auths in a 2h bucket = probing
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner Failed on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (FirstFail .. FirstFail + 24h)
| project FirstFail, SuccessTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, FailCount, FailIPs, SuccessIP = IPAddress, Country, Application
| sort by SuccessTime desc
let Failed = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType !in (0)
| summarize FailCount = count(), FailIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstFail = min(TimeGenerated) by UserPrincipalName, UserId, bin(TimeGenerated, 2h)
| where FailCount >= 3;  // 3+ failed auths in a 2h window
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationMethodsUsed) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner Failed on UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (FirstFail .. FirstFail + 24h)
| project FirstFail, SuccessTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, FailCount, FailIPs, SuccessIP = IPAddress, Location, AppDisplayName
| sort by SuccessTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0 (*FIDO2* OR *Passkey*)
M365 sign-in with recently-enrolled passkey from new user-agent and IP AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts when a successful passkey/FIDO2 sign-in uses a passkey enrolled in the last 24 hours and originates from a user-agent + IP combination never seen for that user in the 30-day baseline. Captures the attacker operating the fraudulently-enrolled passkey from their own browser/device. Rationale: Reviewer-requested. Combines three weak signals into a sharp one: passkey <24h old (fresh rogue enrollment), plus a UA+IP tuple absent from the user's baseline (attacker's own environment). Leftanti baseline expresses 'first-time observed' without ML. Cross-checked against: • https://www.okta.com/blog/threat-intelligence/vishing-actors-target-microsoft-entra-passkey-enrollment-/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/entra-passkey-enrollment-vishing-targets-microsoft-365-users/
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User enrolls a passkey then signs in from a new personal laptop/browser (new UA+IP) legitimately
  • User travels and first uses the new passkey from a hotel/airport IP
  • Browser or OS update changing the user-agent string right after enrollment
  • BYOD device newly used with a corporate passkey
  • Thin baseline for a recently onboarded user
Suppression filter
| where Country != "<home_country_iso_placeholder>" // optional geo refinement; safer to keep UA+IP baseline leftanti as the primary filter
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect UserAgent and IP geo/ASN; a datacenter/VPN ASN or foreign geo on a fresh passkey is high-signal. 2) Contain: revoke tokens, remove the recently-registered passkey, and require verified re-enrollment; enforce a conditional-access session control on the user. 3) Hunt: review the target application activity (mailbox rules, SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, Teams data access) for the data-extortion follow-on this actor is known for.

let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta

AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationDetails) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner RecentReg on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (RegTime .. RegTime + 24h)

| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, UserAgent, Country, Application, RegTime
| sort by Timestamp desc
let RecentReg = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2d)
| where OperationName has "security info" and tostring(TargetResources) has_any ("Fido2","FIDO2","passkey","security key")
| summarize RegTime = max(TimeGenerated) by UserId = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.id);
let Baseline = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserId, UserAgent, IPAddress;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ResultType == 0
| where tostring(AuthenticationMethodsUsed) has_any ("FIDO2","Passkey")
| join kind=inner RecentReg on UserId
| where TimeGenerated between (RegTime .. RegTime + 24h)

| sort by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

logsource:

detection:

ENDPOINT

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
